They performed these and other unrefined actions. But she, accomplished in good manners, walked at a measured pace alongside them. When the girls reached the park, they placed their garments on the bank of the lotus-pond and plunged in hastily, beginning to play. But she — as the water rose, she lifted her garment that much as she descended, and with the same calm deportment, as she came out, she lowered her garment step by step. Then, having bathed and composed herself, she stood in one place. Those girls ate their food first and then began serving the attendants. (

children.text: ) ārabdhāḥ / sāpi pūrvaṃ parijanaṃ pariveṣya paścād ātmanā paribhoktum ārabdhā / tato bhuktapītā udyānasukham anubhūya saṃprasthitā / yāvad antarmārge pānīyam uttartavyaṃ tā dārikā upānahau chorayitvottīrṇāḥ / sā tu sopānatkaiva punaḥ saṃprasthitā / tāsām ārāmasaṃpraveśo jātaḥ / sā chatram ādāya āmravanam atikrāntā / anyābhiś chatrāṇi choritāni / tato vātavarṣaṃ prādurbhutam* / tadā dārikā devakulaṃ praviśyāvasthitā / sā tv abhyavakāśa eva / sa brāhmaṇas tasyās tādṛśalakṣaṇapracārān dṛṣṭvā tato jātakutūhalas tāṃ dārikāṃ praṣṭum ārabdhaḥ / dārike kasya tvam* / balamitrasya duhitā / putri pṛcchāmi / tena kiñcit tvayā kopaḥ karaṇīyaḥ / sā smitapūrvaṃgamā kathayati / tāta pṛccha / ko 'tra kopaḥ / putri sarvā eva dārikā dhāvantya utpatantyo nipatantyo gātravikṣepaṃ kurvantya imāni cānyāni ca durvṛttaceṣṭitāni kurvantyo gacchanti tvaṃ punar vinayasaṃpannā mandagatipracāratayā ābhiḥ (
children.translated_text: ) But she first served the attendants and then began eating herself. After eating and drinking, having enjoyed the pleasures of the park, they set out. Along the way, there was water to cross. The other girls took off their sandals and crossed. But she crossed still wearing her sandals and continued on. When they reached the garden entrance, she took an umbrella and passed through the mango grove. The other girls discarded their umbrellas. Then a storm of wind and rain arose. The other girls entered a temple and took shelter. But she remained in the open. The <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, having observed her character and conduct, filled with curiosity, began to question the girl. 'Girl, whose are you?' 'The daughter of <s>Balamitra</s>.' 'Daughter, I ask — for which you should feel no anger.' She said with a preliminary smile: 'Father, ask. What anger is there here?' 'Daughter, all the other girls went running, jumping, falling, making gestures, and performing these and other unrefined actions, yet you, accomplished in manners, walked at a measured pace with them (
MSV II 55

children.text: ) sārdham udyānaṃ gacchasīti / sā kathayati / sarvā dārikā mātāpitror vikreyaṃ dravyam* / yadi mama utpatantyā nipatantyā vā hastaḥ pādo vā bhidyate ko māṃ prārthayate / na tv ahaṃ yāvajjīvam eva mātāpitroḥ poṣyā bhaviṣyāmi / putri śobhanaṃ gatam etat* / idam aparaṃ pṛcchāmi / etā dārikā vastrāṇy ekānte sthāpayitvā dvitīyavastraviyuktāḥ sahasāvatīrya krīḍitum ārabdhāḥ / tvaṃ punar yathā pānīyam avatarati tathā tathā vastram anayasi / tāta hrīvyapatrāpyasaṃpanno mātṛgrāmaḥ / yadi māṃ kaścit paśyaty apāvṛtām ayuktam* / putri kas tvāṃ tatra paśyati / tāta tvayaiva tāvad ahaṃ dṛṣṭā syām* / putri śobhanam etad api gatam* / idam aparaṃ pṛcchāmi / etā dārikāḥ pūrvam ātmanā bhuktvā paścāt parijanaṃ bhojayanti / tvaṃ punaḥ pūrvaṃ parijanaṃ bhojayitvā paścād ātmanā bhuṃkṣe / tāta vayaṃ puṇyaphalopajīvinyaḥ satatam evāsmākaṃ parva / etā kusthānaphalopajīvinyaḥ kadācit karhicid udārabhojanaṃ labhante / putri śobhanam etad api gatam* / idam aparaṃ pṛcchāmi / sarvalokaḥ śuṣke upānahau dhārayanti / tvaṃ punaḥ udake / kim etat* / tāta mūrkho lokaḥ / udaka eva upānahau dhārayitavyau / yat kāraṇaṃ sthale sthāṇur dṛśyate kaṇṭakaḥ pāśāṇaśarkaraḥ śuktiśakalikā śaṃkhasūke khaṇḍikā ca / (
children.translated_text: ) to the park. Why?' She said: 'All girls are merchandise to be sold by their parents. If while jumping or falling, my hand or foot breaks, who would want me? Nor shall I remain forever to be supported by my parents.' 'Daughter, well answered. Now I ask another thing. These girls placed their clothes in one spot and, without a second garment, plunged in hastily to play. But you — as the water rose, you lifted your garment accordingly.' 'Father, womanhood is endowed with modesty and shame. If someone were to see me uncovered — that would be improper.' 'Daughter, who would see you there?' 'Father, you yourself would have seen me!' 'Daughter, well answered that too. Now I ask another thing. These girls ate their food first and then fed the attendants. But you first fed the attendants and then ate yourself.' 'Father, we live on the fruits of merit. Every day is a festival for us. These others live on the fruits of menial work. Only occasionally do they obtain a good meal.' 'Daughter, well answered that too. Now I ask another thing. Everyone wears sandals on dry ground. But you — in the water. Why is that?' 'Father, the world is foolish. Sandals should be worn in water. The reason is: on dry ground, one can see stumps, thorns, pebbles, shell-fragments, conch-pieces, and shards. (
MSV II 56

children.text: ) jale tv ete na dṛśyante / ato jala evopānahau dhārayitavyā na sthale / putri śobhanam etad api gatam* / idam aparaṃ pṛcchāmi / etā dārikā ātape chatraṃ dhārayanti tvaṃ punar ārāme vṛkṣacchāyāyām* / kātra yuktiḥ / tāta mūrkho lokaḥ / ārāma eva chatraṃ dhārayitavyam* / yat kāraṇaṃ nityam ārāmaḥ śākhāmṛgaiḥ pakṣibhir ākīrṇaḥ / pakṣiṇa uccāraprasrāvaṃ kurvanti / asthikhaṇḍaṃ pātayanti / śākhāmṛgā uccāraprasrāvaṃ kurvanti / ardhaparibhuktāni phalāni pātayanti / calasvabhāvatvād itaś cāmutaś ca śākhāntare saṃkrāmaṃ kurvanti / kāṣṭhakhaṇḍāni pātayanti / abhyavakāśe ca tan nāsti / kadācit syāt taṃtu laghunipāti / ata ārāma eva chatraṃ dhārayitavyaṃ (
children.translated_text: ) But in water, these are not visible. Therefore, sandals should be worn in water, not on dry ground.' 'Daughter, well answered that too. Now I ask another thing. These girls held an umbrella in the sunshine, but you in the garden, under the shade of trees. What is the reason?' 'Father, the world is foolish. An umbrella should be held in the garden. The reason is: a garden is always full of monkeys and birds. Birds make droppings, and drop bone-fragments. Monkeys make droppings and drop half-eaten fruits. Being restless by nature, they leap from one branch to another, dropping pieces of wood. But in the open, this does not happen. Occasionally there might be, but it falls lightly. Therefore, an umbrella should be held in the garden, (

children.text: ) nābhyavakāśe / putri śobhanam etad api gatam* / idam aparaṃ pṛcchāmi / etā dārikā vātavarṣe devakulaṃ praviṣṭās tvaṃ punar abhyavakāśe sthitā / tāta abhyavakāśa eva sthātavyam* / na devakulaṃ praveṣṭavyam* / putri kātra yuktiḥ / tāta etāni śūnyadevakulāni nityam eva viṭavātaputradhūrtakair aśūnyāni / yadi mama praviṣṭāyā kaścid aṃgapratyaṃgāni parāmṛśati na tv evaṃ mātāpitror me ayaśasyatā bhavati / varam abhyavakāśe prāṇaviyogaḥ / na tv eva śūnyadevakulapraveśaḥ /
children.translated_text: ) not in the open.' 'Daughter, well answered that too. Now I ask another thing. These girls entered a temple during the storm of wind and rain, but you stood in the open.' 'Father, one should stand in the open. One should not enter a temple.' 'Daughter, what is the reason?' 'Father, these empty temples are always full of rogues, vagrants, and scoundrels. If, having entered, someone were to touch my limbs — would there not be disgrace for my parents? Better to lose one's life in the open than to enter an empty temple.'

body.translated_text: In <s>Campā</s> there was a householder named <s>Balamitra</s>. He had a daughter named <s>Viśākhā</s> — endowed with beauty and youth, accomplished in conduct and good manners, wise, and shrewd in her ways. She set out for the park grounds with maidens who were attractive as she desired. That <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> had come to that very place. He saw that girl. He reflected: 'Let me first test these girls.' He, attentive and observant, followed behind them at a slow pace. Women are generally fickle by nature. (

body.text: tato 'sau brāhmaṇas tatpracārāvarjitajanitasaumanasyo balamitrasya gṛhapater niveśanaṃ praviśya kanyāpratilambhatṛṣṇāyā sasaṃbhramaḥ svasti svastīty uvāca / gṛhaparijanaḥ kathayati / brāhmaṇa na tāvad bhikṣāvelā / kiṃ prārthayase / kanyābhikṣām* / kasyārthāya / śrāvastyāṃ mṛgāro nāmāgrāmātyaḥ / tasya putro viśākho nāma / te kathayanti / sadṛśam asmākaṃ tat kulam* / kiṃ tarhi / ativiprakṛṣṭo deśaḥ / sa kathayati / dūra eva dārikā dātavyā / kiṃ kāraṇam* / yadi tāvat sukhitā bhavati śrutvā prāmodyam utpādayiṣyati / atha duḥkhitā dānamānasatkārakriyayā khedam āpadyate 'rthāpacayaś ca bhavati / te kathayanti / yady evaṃ dattā bhavatu / tato brāhmaṇaḥ svastīty uktvā prakrānto 'nupūrveṇa śrāvastīṃ gataḥ / mārgaśramaṃ prativinodya mṛgārāgrāmātyasya sakāśaṃ gataḥ / tato dārikāyā āhāravihāratāṃ ceṣṭāṃ rūpayauvanaśobhāṃ vaicakṣaṇyaṃ ca yathāvadākhyāya kathayati / mayā mahatā parikhedena nānādigdeśādhiṣṭhānān paryaṭitvā sā kṛcchreṇa pratilabdhā / gacchedānīṃ pariṇayeti / tato mṛgāreṇāgrāmātyena divasatithimuhūrtanakṣatrapratigrahaṃ kṛtvā caṇpām āgatya mahatā śrīsamudayena viśākhasya pariṇītā /
body.translated_text: Then that <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, his mind delighted and filled with joy at her conduct, entered the house of the householder <s>Balamitra</s> and, eagerly desirous of obtaining the girl, exclaimed: 'Blessings! Blessings!' The household attendants said: '<s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, it is not yet time for alms. What do you seek?' 'I seek the alms of a maiden.' 'For whose sake?' 'In <s>Śrāvastī</s> there is a chief minister named <s>Mṛgāra</s>. He has a son named <s>Viśākha</s>.' They said: 'That family is a suitable match for us. But the country is very far away.' He said: 'A daughter should be given far away. What is the reason? If she is happy, hearing of it will give joy. If she is unhappy, one will be spared the distress of gifts, hospitality, and visits — and there will be no expenditure of wealth.' They said: 'If so, let her be given.' Then the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, having said 'Blessings!' departed and in due course reached <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having rested from the fatigue of the journey, he went to the chief minister <s>Mṛgāra</s>, duly reported the girl's diet, conduct, behavior, beauty, youth, beauty, and cleverness, and said: 'With great effort, wandering through various countries and regions, I have obtained her with difficulty. Go now and marry her.' Then the chief minister <s>Mṛgāra</s>, having determined the auspicious day, hour, and constellation, went to <s>Campā</s> and married <s>Viśākhā</s> for his son with great splendor.

body.text: sā mātrā gamanadeśakāle śikṣyate / putri nityaṃ tvayā sūryācandramasau namasyau / agniḥ paricartavyaḥ / ādarśo nirmādayitavyaḥ / śuklāni vāsāṃsi prāvaritavyāni / grahītavyaṃ na dātavyam* / vāṇī (

children.translated_text: ) should be guarded. One should not give up one's seat for anyone. Delicious food should be eaten. One should sleep comfortably. A ladder should be bound.' Then <s>Mṛgāra</s> heard this. He reflected: 'This girl holds wrong views. I shall separate her from her wrong views and establish her in right view.' Having understood this, he took her and set out.

body.translated_text: Her mother instructed her at the time of departure: 'Daughter, you should always worship the sun and moon. The fire should be tended. The mirror should be polished. White garments should be worn. One should receive, not give. Speech (

body.text: tato 'syā mātā snehavyākulahṛdayā aśruvyākulekṣaṇā kaṇṭhe pariṣvajya sasvaraṃ rudantī kathayati / putri idaṃ te paścimaṃ darśanam iti / sā tām anusaṃjñāpayantī kathayati / amba pṛcchāmi / tāvat kiṃ tvam atra jātāhosvij jñātigṛhe /

children.translated_text: 'Daughter, in my relatives' house.'

children.text: tat tava gṛham āhosvid idam* / idam* / aham apīha jātā / tatra mayā vastavyam* / saṃyogo niyataṃ viyogāntaḥ / tūṣṇīṃbhava / kimarthaṃ rodiṣi /
children.translated_text: 'Then is your home there or here?' 'Here.' 'I too was born here. I must live there. Union inevitably ends in separation. Be at peace. Why do you weep?'

body.translated_text: Then her mother, her heart agitated with affection, her eyes filled with tears, embracing her neck, weeping aloud, said: 'Daughter, this is your last sight of me.' She, consoling her mother, said: 'Mother, I ask — were you born here or in your relatives' house?'

children.translated_text: ) distress, they thought. She, despite all efforts, would not board, and an uproar arose. <s>Viśākhā</s> heard it. She said: 'Why is there this uproar?' They told her what had happened. <s>Viśākhā</s> said: 'First make the foal board—she will board on her own.' They did so. She boarded. Then <s>Mṛgāra</s> asked them: 'Why have you come so late?' 'The mare (
MSV II 59

children.text: ) nāvaṃ nābhirohati / atha katham abhirūḍhā / cāṇpeyikayā upāyasaṃvidhānam ākhyātaṃ kiśorakaṃ pūrvam abhirohayata / paṇḍitā cāṇpeyikā /
children.translated_text: ) would not board the boat.' 'Then how did she board?' 'The <s>Cāṇpeyikā</s> (girl from <s>Campā</s>) devised a stratagem: "First make the foal board."' 'The <s>Cāṇpeyikā</s> is clever!'

body.translated_text: Then <s>Mṛgāra</s> set out by land. <s>Viśākhā</s> set out by boat together with her husband and the household servants obtained from her own family. There, a mare that had recently given birth was being made to board the boat. The foal, [left] on land, would suffer (

body.text: yāvad antarmārgo sārthā rātriṃ vāsam upagatāḥ / mṛgārasya prāgbhāre śayyā prajñaptā / viśākhā dṛṣṭvā pṛcchati / kasyaiṣā śayyā / mṛgārasya / apanayata / kiṃ kāraṇam* / yadi suptasya prāgbhāra upari nipatati niyatam avaṣṭabdhaḥ kālaṃ karoti / mama yāvajjīvam ayaśasyam* / īdṛśī dārikā pariṇītā yad antarmārga eva śvaśuraḥ kālagato gṛham api na saṃprāpta iti / tac ca śayanāsanam apanītaṃ prāgbhāraś ca patitaḥ / samantān mahājanakāyaḥ pradhāvito gṛhapatir avaṣṭabdhaḥ iti / gṛhapatiḥ kathayati / bhavanto mā bibhīta / ihāhaṃ tiṣṭhāmi / śayyāṃ pratyavaikṣanta / apanītā śayyā / kena / viśākhayā / paṇḍitā cāṇpeyikā / punar api jīrṇodyāne vāsam upagatāḥ / mṛgārasya śūnyadevakule śayyā prajñaptā / viśākhayā dṛṣṭā / pṛcchati / kasyaiṣā śayyā / āryasya / apanayata / kiṃ kāraṇām* / yadi devakulaṃ patati tato 'vaṣṭabdhaḥ kālaṃ karoti / nanu me pūrvavad yaśasyam* / sā cāpanitā / devakulaṃ ca patitam* / mahājanakāyo pradhāvitaḥ pūrvavad yāvat paṇḍitā cāṇpeyikā /
body.translated_text: While on the road, the caravan stopped for the night. A bed was prepared for <s>Mṛgāra</s> under a projecting balcony. <s>Viśākhā</s>, seeing it, asked: 'Whose bed is this?' '<s>Mṛgāra</s>'s.' 'Remove it.' 'Why?' 'If the balcony falls upon him while he sleeps, he will surely be crushed and die. It would be a lifelong disgrace for me—"Such a girl was married, and yet her father-in-law died on the road itself, without even reaching home."' The bed was removed, and the balcony collapsed. From all sides a great crowd rushed over: 'The householder has been crushed!' The householder said: 'Sirs, do not be alarmed. I am here.' They looked at the bed—it had been removed. 'By whom?' 'By <s>Viśākhā</s>.' 'The <s>Cāṇpeyikā</s> is clever!' Again, they stopped at a ruined garden. A bed was prepared for <s>Mṛgāra</s> in an abandoned temple. <s>Viśākhā</s> saw it. She asked: 'Whose bed is this?' 'The master's.' 'Remove it.' 'Why?' 'If the temple collapses, he will be crushed and die. Surely that would bring me the same disgrace as before.' It too was removed. The temple collapsed. A great crowd rushed over as before, until [they said]: 'The <s>Cāṇpeyikā</s> is clever!'

body.text: yāvad anupūrveṇa śrāvastīm anuprāptā / mārgaśrame prativinodite suhṛtsaṃbandhibāndhavajane ca preṣite viśākhā svakulānurūpaṃ gṛhe (

children.translated_text: MSV II 60

children.text: ) karma kāryate / mṛgārasya ṣaṭ snuṣā vāreṇa vāraṃ gṛhajanasya bhaktaṃ saṃpādayanti / viśākhāpi tathaiva niyuktā / tvayāpi saptame divase vāraḥ kartavya iti / tasyā vāra āgamiṣyatīti / ye śvaśuraśvaśrūsvāmināṃ gandhā avaśiṣyante carpaṭikāṃ kṛtvā pratidivasaṃ śoṣayati / yān saktūn pratidinaṃ labhate tataḥ prasthāni viśākhā apanīya sthāpayati / pariśiṣṭaṃ ghṛtena modayati tatpramāṇā eva bhavanti / madyapānāgatas tu śvo vāro bhaviṣyatīti / yat svāmino nirmālyam ātmanaś ca tacchītale sthāpitam* / yāvat prabhātāyāṃ rajanyāṃ karmakarāṇāṃ āmalakaṃ dattaṃ gandhaḥ puṣpāṇi bhojanaṃ madyaṃ ca / te parituṣṭāś cireṇa vayaṃ purāṇagṛhapatipatnyā avalokitā iti / tais tasmin divase dviguṇaṃ karma kṛtam* / yāvan mṛgāraḥ kālavelāyāṃ karmāntān avalokayan paśyati prabhūtaṃ karma kṛtam* / sa pṛcchati / kiṃ yuṣmābhir apare bhṛtakapuruṣā gṛhītāḥ / na / kenacit ko 'tra yogo yenādya dviguṇaṃ karma kṛtam* / te kathayanti / āryā yādṛśaṃ bhaktaṃ tādṛśaṃ karma / kim etat* / tair yathāvṛttaṃ vistareṇa samākhyātam* / mṛgāraputrais svakasvakānāṃ patnyaḥ (
children.translated_text: ) began managing the household affairs. <s>Mṛgāra</s>'s six daughters-in-law took turns preparing food for the household. <s>Viśākhā</s> too was similarly appointed: 'You too shall have your turn on the seventh day.' Her turn was about to come. The perfumes left over from her father-in-law, mother-in-law, and husband she made into cakes and dried daily. The grain-flour she received each day, <s>Viśākhā</s> set aside by the measure and stored it. The remainder she sweetened with ghee—they were of the same quantity. On the evening before [her day], having returned from the drinking party, whatever flower-garlands were discarded by her husband and herself, she kept in a cool place. When dawn came, she gave the workers <s>āmalaka</s> fruit, perfumes, flowers, food, and liquor. They were delighted: 'At last we have been looked after by the young mistress of the household!' On that day they did double the work. When <s>Mṛgāra</s> inspected the work output at the proper time, he saw that a great deal of work had been done. He asked: 'Have you hired additional laborers?' 'No.' 'Then what method was used that double the work was done today?' They said: 'As the food, so the work.' 'What does this mean?' They told him in full detail what had happened. <s>Mṛgāra</s>'s sons told their respective wives (
MSV II 61

children.translated_text: ) just as <s>Viśākhā</s> did.' Then <s>Mṛgāra</s> asked <s>Viśākhā</s>: 'Daughter, how did you manage the food so skillfully?' She told him in full detail. <s>Mṛgāra</s> was pleased. He appointed her alone to manage household affairs. And the entire inner household was told: 'Whoever among you is satisfied with what <s>Viśākhā</s> provides must stay, or else behave agreeably'—and so she became the mistress of the household. By her proper conduct and gentle disposition, she delighted the entire inner household. At another time, geese flying over <s>Viśākhā</s>'s house from <s>Uttarakuru-dvīpa</s>, carrying self-sown rice with fruit-bearing stalks, set out [overhead]. Now, in the king's house there was a [domesticated] goose. Seeing those [wild geese], it called out. Those [wild geese] too, unable to bear the agitation caused by trust in one of their own species, called out [in return]. Rice-stalks fell into the king's foot-washing basin. The king gave one [stalk] to each minister. <s>Mṛgāra</s> gave his share to <s>Viśākhā</s>. She stored it in a casket and gave orders to the farmers. They were exceedingly delighted. They carefully plowed a small field, determined the right season, and sowed it. The rain-god rained at the proper time. A harvest fitting to the seed was produced. The following year there was an abundant crop, and the year after that even more abundant. (
MSV II 62
) Thus, in time, all the granaries were filled with goose-brought grain bins. {MS

children.translated_text: } They were completely filled. Then King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> fell ill. He summoned physicians and asked them. They said: 'Your Majesty, if goose-brought rice can be obtained, you should prepare gruel from it. After drinking it, you will recover.' The king summoned the ministers and asked: 'Sirs, I gave you goose-brought rice-heads. What did you do with them?' Some said: 'Your Majesty, we offered them at a temple.' Others said: 'We threw them into the fire.' Others said: 'We tied them at the doorway.' <s>Mṛgāra</s> said: 'Your Majesty, I gave mine to <s>Viśākhā</s>. Let me ask what she did with them.' He asked <s>Viśākhā</s>. She said: 'Father, what need is there for goose-brought rice?' 'The king has fallen ill. The physicians have prescribed goose-brought rice.' Then <s>Viśākhā</s> [filled] a golden vessel with goose-brought rice
gruel,

children.translated_text: ) They began to investigate. One was asked. He said: 'It is mine.' The other was asked. He said: 'It is mine.' 'Yours!' 'Mine!'—and so the whole day passed. The ministers, exhausted, went home late without having resolved it. <s>Viśākhā</s> asked <s>Mṛgāra</s> as before. He told her what had happened. <s>Viśākhā</s> said: 'Father, what is there to determine? Tell them both: let one take half and the other take half. The true owner will say: "Why is my blanket being cut?" The one who is not the owner will think: "Let me at least have half—what loss is there for me?" This is the test.' <s>Mṛgāra</s> went and reported to the ministers. [They tested it.] As before, until the king said: 'The <s>Cāṇpeyikā</s> is clever!'

body.translated_text: A certain man, having placed his blanket at a bathing ford, was bathing. Another man arrived. He wrapped his head in that blanket and began bathing right there. The first man, having bathed and gotten up, did not see his blanket. The [second] man said: 'Sir, what are you looking for?' 'My blanket.' 'How would you have a blanket? Perhaps you entered [the water] with your head wrapped, just as I entered with mine.' He said: 'That is indeed my blanket!' 'Yours!' 'Mine!'—and so a dispute arose between them. They went before the king. The king ordered the ministers: 'Sirs, investigate and give it to the one to whom it belongs.' (

body.text: rājño yānapātrakeṇa vaṇijā candanagaṇḍīrakaḥ prāvṛto 'nupreṣitaḥ / tasya na vijñāyate katarad agraṃ kataran mūlam iti / rājā amātyānām ājñā dattā / vicārayatha iti / taiḥ kṛtsnaṃ divasaṃ vicāritam* / na parijñātam* / cirakāle gṛhaṃ gatāḥ / viśākhayā pūrvavad yāvan mṛgāraḥ pṛṣṭaḥ / tena yathāvṛttaṃ vistareṇa samākyātam* / viśākhā kathayati / tāta kim atra jñātavyam* / udake prakṣeptavyaḥ / yan mūlaṃ tad adhastād bhavati / yad agraṃ tad upariṣṭād bhavati / eṣā tatra parīkṣeti / mṛgāreṇa amātyānāṃ niveditam* / pūrvavad yāvad rājā kathayati / paṇḍitā cāṇpeyiketi /
body.translated_text: By the king's ship, a merchant sent a sandalwood log wrapped up. They could not determine which end was the top and which the root. The king ordered the ministers: 'Investigate.' They deliberated the entire day. It could not be determined. They went home late. <s>Viśākhā</s> asked <s>Mṛgāra</s> as before. He told her everything in detail. <s>Viśākhā</s> said: 'Father, what is there to determine? Throw it in water. The root end will sink lower; the top end will float higher. This is the test.' <s>Mṛgāra</s> reported to the ministers. As before, until the king said: 'The <s>Cāṇpeyikā</s> is clever!'

children.translated_text: ) He was raised by her. His father also died. A dispute arose between the two women on account of the house. One said: 'He is indeed my son.' The other said: 'He is my son.' They went before the king. The king gave an order to the ministers: 'Go, sirs, and investigate.' While they were investigating, the day passed but the matter was not resolved. After a long time they went home. <s>Viśākhā</s> asked <s>Mṛgāra</s>—as before, in full detail—'What is to be determined here?' They should be told: 'We do not know whose son he is. Let whichever of you two is stronger take him and go.' The two women seized him by both arms and pulled. He, being in pain, (

When she is beaten with whips, she will tell the truth. This is the test.' <s>Mṛgāra</s> informed the ministers thus. As before, in full detail, the king said: 'The <s>Cāmpeyikā</s> girl is wise.'

body.translated_text: In a certain market-town there was a householder. He brought a wife from a family equal to his own. He had neither son nor daughter. Desiring a son, he brought a second wife. The first wife, out of her jealous nature, administered a womb-destroying potion to her. But [instead] her womb was thoroughly purified, and she became pregnant. After the passage of nine months, she gave birth. A boy was born. She [the second wife] reflected: 'The most terrible of enmities is that of a co-wife. Surely the other mother will kill him by some means or other. What will my husband do? What can I do? And for how long must he be protected? In any case, he should be given to her [the first wife] herself.' Having deliberated with her husband and obtained his consent, she addressed the first wife: 'Sister, this son is given to you by me. Raise him.' She [the first wife] reflected: 'She who has the son has the household. I shall raise him. I shall be the mistress of the house.' (

body.text: athāpareṇa samayena mṛgāro glānipatitaḥ / tasya vaidya ekaṃ divasaṃ bhaiṣajyaṃ dadāti punar glāno bhavati / viśākhā saṃlakṣayati / kimarthaṃ tāta ekasmin divase svastho bhavati dvitīye divase punar glāno bhavati / yair bhaiṣajyaiḥ svastho bhavati tāni nimittīkṛtāni / tatas tayā vaidyānāṃ dvāraṃ dhārayitvā svayam eva cikitsā kṛtā / svasthībhūtaḥ / mṛgāraḥ saṃlakṣayati / ko 'tra yogo yenāham ekasmin divase svastho bhavāmy ekasmin glānaḥ / yadā vaidyo na praviśati tadā nityam eva svastha iti / tena viśākhā pṛṣṭā / pūrvavad yāvat paṇḍitā cāṇpeyikā /
body.translated_text: At another time, <s>Mṛgāra</s> fell ill. His physician would give him medicine one day, then he would fall ill again. <s>Viśākhā</s> observed: 'Why is father well one day and ill again the next?' She noted which medicines made him well. Then, barring the physicians from entry, she herself performed the treatment. He recovered. <s>Mṛgāra</s> reflected: 'What is this circumstance—that I am well one day and ill the next? When the physician does not come in, I am always well.' He asked <s>Viśākhā</s>. As before, in full detail: 'The <s>Cāmpeyikā</s> girl is wise.'

children.translated_text: ) him.' The king said: 'Pardoned.' 'Lord, if he is pardoned, let his stipends be restored to him.' 'So be it.' They were restored. <s>Śrīvardhana</s> learned that <s>Viśākhā</s> had caused the king to pardon him. He resolved to repay her kindness. At another time, <s>Mṛgāra</s> developed a genital disease. <s>Viśākhā</s> attended to him. He felt ashamed. She said: 'Father, why are you ashamed? Does a daughter not attend to her father?' But still he felt ashamed. She reflected: 'He will not accept nursing from me. I shall arrange a wife for him.' She went to <s>Śrīvardhana</s>'s house. He greeted her with words of welcome and offered a seat. <s>Śrīvardhana</s>'s daughter was seated there. He told her: 'Girl, clasp <s>Viśākhā</s>'s feet.' <s>Viśākhā</s> said: 'There may come a time when I myself shall clasp her feet,' and said: 'Blessings, daughter.' <s>Śrīvardhana</s> said: 'What do you desire?' 'A gift of a maiden.' 'For whose sake?' She said: 'For father's.' He fell silent. <s>Śrīvardhana</s>'s wife said: 'He is old. How can she be given to him?' <s>Viśākhā</s> said: 'Men are measured by their wealth and vigor. Why deliberate? When she says "the sun and moon are to be worshiped"—for a girl, the sun and moon represent her parents-in-law; them I worship. When she says "the fire is to be tended"—for a wife, her husband stands in the place of fire; one must stay near one's husband, not too far away; so I tend my husband as I would tend fire. When she says "the mirror is to be polished"—the house stands in the place of a mirror; it must always be plastered and swept; so I maintain the house daily. When she says "white garments are to be worn"—household work should be done in other clothes; having put on white garments, one should attend to worship and approach one's own adornment; this too I do. When she says "one should receive but not give"—what is to be received? Harsh words from people; and no harsh word should be spoken back; this too I observe. When she says "speech is to be guarded"—secret matters should not be revealed; I do exercise restraint of speech. When she says "no one should be given a seat by rising"—this means: you are a woman of good family; you should sit in a secluded place; so I sit only in secluded places. When she says "eat daintily"—one should eat when truly hungry; so I always eat after the household has eaten, when I am truly hungry. body.translated_text: Then <s>Mṛgāra</s> thought: 'If the Blessed One would give permission, I would proclaim <s>Viśākhā</s> as Mother.' Having resolved this, he went to the Blessed One. Having approached and bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, he said: 'Venerable sir, is it permissible to proclaim one's daughter-in-law as Mother?' The Blessed One said: 'If she is endowed with five qualities. Which five? She tends the sick; she establishes family members in suitable marriages; she protects them with her life; she guards their wealth; and she makes arrangements with wisdom.'

And a messenger came from the king to them: 'Let the boys come.' Then the king, having incapacitated them with <s>hālāhala</s> poison mixed with [food], cut off their heads. Then, filling a box and placing the head of the eldest son on top, sealing it with a wax seal, he sent it to <s>Viśākhā</s>. <s>Viśākhā</s> thought: 'Surely the king has sent garments for the nephews. I too shall provide garments for the <s>Saṅgha</s> of monks headed by the <s>Buddha</s>.' Then, knowing that the <s>Saṅgha</s> of monks headed by the <s>Buddha</s> was comfortably seated, she served them with pure and choice hard and soft foods, as before in full detail, and knowing that the Blessed One had eaten, with his hands washed and his bowl removed, she began to open the box. The Blessed One reflected: 'If <s>Viśākhā</s>, who has not yet seen the Truths, sees the killing of her sons, there is a possibility that she will become unworthy of the Truths.' Having understood this, the Blessed One said to <s>Viśākhā</s>: 'Sit down first and listen to the <s>Dharma</s>. Afterward you may do as you wish.' She, having bowed at the Blessed One's feet, sat before him to listen to the <s>Dharma</s>. Then the Blessed One, knowing her disposition, latent tendencies, nature, and temperament, as before in full detail, brought about her vision of the Truths. Then, having seen the Truths, she opened the box and saw the heads of her sons. Then she said: 'Blessed One, thus indeed all <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned things) are impermanent.' That young woman was present right there. Having performed worship, they made a vow: "By this root of merit, may we become great, foremost in strength." She asked them: "Sons, what vow have you made?" They said: "Mother, this and this." She said: "Sons, if so, may I be your mother." They said: "Mother, so be it." Having said this, they departed. She reflected: "That woman, giving birth just once, cries out afflicted by the pain of labor. But I, giving birth thirty-two times, what shall I do?" While she was deliberating thus, near the <s>stūpa</s>, a hen gave birth. In just a moment, she laid thirty-two eggs without crying out. She reflected: "This is a good method of giving birth!" Then, having fallen before that <s>stūpa</s> with intense faith, she began to make a vow: "Just as this hen in a mere moment gave birth to thirty-two eggs, so may I too give birth to thirty-two eggs at once."

body.translated_text: 'Once upon a time, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a certain householder's son died. His wife was one who always longed for sons. When the Blessed One <s>Kāśyapa</s>, the Perfectly Enlightened <s>Buddha</s>, having completed all his <s>Buddha</s>-work, passed into the <s>nirvāṇa</s>-element without remainder, like fire [going out] when fuel is exhausted—at that time, in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, there was a king named <s>Kṛki</s>. He had established a <s>stūpa</s> of four [kinds of] jewels for the Blessed One <s>Kāśyapa</s>, the Perfectly Enlightened <s>Buddha</s>. That childless young woman who always longed for sons had grown old. Having performed service at that <s>stūpa</s>, she remained there. Having made an offering of alms at that <s>stūpa</s>, she made a vow: "By the merit of my having performed

body.text: kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ / yā sā vṛddhā yuvatir eṣaiva sā viśākhā / tena kālena tena samayena ye te dvātriṃśad goṣṭhikā eta eva te dvātriṃśad viśākhāputrāḥ / yad anayā tatra praṇidhānaṃ kṛtaṃ tasya karmaṇo vipākena dvātriṃśadaṇḍāni prasūtāni /
body.translated_text: 'What do you think, monks? That old young woman—she is none other than this <s>Viśākhā</s>. The thirty-two guild members at that time—they are none other than these thirty-two sons of <s>Viśākhā</s>. Because she made that vow there, by the ripening of that <s>karma</s>, thirty-two eggs were born [to her].'

children.translated_text: and also smelled the male reproductive fluid. Inconceivable is the ripening of beings' <s>karma</s>! She became pregnant. In due course, she came to that very spot and gave birth. A boy was born. Having smelled him and [recognizing him as] a being of a different species, she abandoned him and departed. Then that <s>ṛṣi</s>, while wandering around the hermitage, saw the boy. He began to investigate: 'Whose son is this?' Eventually he saw [that it was] his own. He brought the boy into the hermitage, nursed him, nourished him, and raised him. Since the boy's head resembled that of a deer, the name <s>Mṛgaśiras</s> ('Deer-head') was given to him. In due course, the <s>ṛṣi</s> died. <s>Mṛgaśiras</s> had learned the art of skull-tapping divination. By tapping a skull, he could predict everything. If the sound was rattling and upward-moving, he would predict rebirth among the gods. If it was a middle tone and upward-moving, he would predict rebirth among humans. This was the sign of a good destiny.

children.text: ) bhagavatā vyākṛtaḥ / eṣa bhikṣus trayāṇāṃ saṃyojanānāṃ prahāṇād rāgadveṣamohānāṃ ca tanutvāt sakṛdāgāmī bhaviṣyati / sakṛd imaṃ lokam āgatya duḥkhasyāntaṃ kariṣyatīti / so 'pi kadācit* śrāvastīm āgamiṣyati / sa madīyam āgantukabhaktaṃ pūrvavad yāvat* varṣāśāṭīcīvaraṃ bhikṣuṇī codakaśāṭikām iti / śrutvā ca punar adhigamiṣyāmi prītiprāmodyam udāraṃ kuśalaṃ naiṣkramyopasaṃhitam* / amuko bhikṣuḥ sa bhagavatā vyākṛtaḥ / eṣa bhikṣuḥ paṃcānām avarabhāgīyānāṃ saṃyojanānāṃ prahāṇād anāgāmī / bhaviṣyaty anāgantā punar imaṃ lokam iti / so 'pi kadācit* śrāvastīm āgamiṣyati punaś ca gamiṣyati / sa madīyam āgantukabhaktaṃ pūrvavad yāvad varṣāśāṭīcīvaraṃ bhikṣuṇī codakaśāṭikām iti / śrutvā ca punar adhigamiṣyāmi prītiprāmodyam udāraṃ kuśalaṃ naiṣkramyopasaṃhitam* / amuko bhikṣuḥ sa bhagavatā vyākṛtaḥ / eṣa bhikṣuḥ sarvakleśaprahāṇād arhatvaṃ sākṣātkṛtvā nirupadhiśeṣe nirvāṇadhātau pravekṣyatīti / so 'pi kadācit* śrāvastīm āgamiṣyati punaś ca gamiṣyati / sa madīyam āgantukabhaktaṃ pūrvavad yāvad varṣāśāṭīcīvaraṃ bhikṣuṇī codakaśāṭikām iti / śrutvā ca punar adhigamiṣyāmi prītiprāmodyam udāraṃ kuśalaṃ naiṣkramyopasaṃhitam* / atha bhagavān viśākhāṃ mṛgāramātaraṃ dharmyayā kathayā saṃdarśya samādāpya samuttejya saṃpraharṣyotthāyāsanāt prakrāntaḥ /
children.translated_text: has been declared by the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'This monk, through the abandonment of the three fetters and the diminishing of attachment, hatred, and delusion, will become a once-returner (<s>sakṛdāgāmin</s>). Having come to this world once more, he will make an end of suffering.'" He too will sometime come to <s>Śrāvastī</s>. He will partake of my gift for arriving [monks], as before, up to the rain-bathing robe, and a nun likewise the bathing cloth. And having heard, I shall attain noble joy and gladness, wholesome and connected with renunciation. "Such-and-such a monk has been declared by the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'This monk, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, will become a non-returner (<s>anāgāmin</s>). He will not return again to this world.'" He too will sometime come to <s>Śrāvastī</s> and again depart. He will partake of my gift for arriving [monks], as before, up to the rain-bathing robe, and a nun likewise the bathing cloth. And having heard, I shall attain noble joy and gladness, wholesome and connected with renunciation. "Such-and-such a monk has been declared by the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'This monk, through the abandonment of all afflictions, having directly realized <s>arhatship</s>, will enter the <s>Nirvāṇa</s>-realm without residue.'" He too will sometime come to <s>Śrāvastī</s> and again depart. He will partake of my gift for arriving [monks], as before, up to the rain-bathing robe, and a nun likewise the bathing cloth. And having heard, I shall attain noble joy and gladness, wholesome and connected with renunciation.' Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened <s>Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā</s> with a talk on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.

body.translated_text: <s>Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā</s> heard that the <s>Bhagavān</s>, traveling on a journey through the <s>Kosala</s> country, had arrived at <s>Śrāvastī</s> and was dwelling in their own monastery. Having heard, she approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>.

body.text: atha bhagavān yathābhiramya śrāvastyāṃ viharati / yena vaiśālī tena cārikāṃ prakrāntaḥ / anupūrveṇa cārikāṃ caran vaiśālīm anuprāptaḥ / vaiśālyāṃ viharati markaṭahradatīre kūṭāgāraśālāyām* / atha bhagavān pūrvāhṇe nivāsya pātracīvaram ādāya vaiśālīṃ piṇḍāya prāvikṣat* (

children.translated_text: [MSV II 88]

children.text: ) tena khalu samayena saṃbahulā bhikṣava ārāmadvāre aśucimrakṣitāni śayanāsanāni śocayanty ātāpayanti praviṣajanti / adrākṣīd bhagavān saṃbahulān bhikṣūn ārāmadvāre aśucimrakṣitāni śayanāsanāni śocayata ātapayataḥ praviṣajataḥ / dṛṣṭvā ca punar asyaitad abhavat* / yad api śrāddhā brāhmaṇagṛhapatayaḥ prapīḍya prapīḍya tvaṅmāṃsaśoṇitaṃ dānāni dadati puṇyāni kurvanti tad api bhikṣavo mātrayā pratisaṃkhyāya paribhuṃjanta iti viditvā vaiśālīṃ piṇḍāya caritvā kṛtabhaktakṛtyaḥ paścādbhaktapiṇḍapātapratikrāntaḥ pātracīvaraṃ pratiśāmayya pādau prakṣālya vihāraṃ prāvikṣat pratisaṃlayanāya / atha bhagavān sāyāhne pratisaṃlayanād vyutthāya purastād bhikṣusaṃghasya prajñapta evāsane niṣaṇṇaḥ / (
children.translated_text: At that time, many monks were at the monastery gate, cleaning, airing, and drying bedding and seating that had been soiled with impurities. The <s>Bhagavān</s> saw the many monks at the monastery gate cleaning, airing, and drying the bedding and seating soiled with impurities. Having seen this, he reflected: 'Although faithful <s>brāhmaṇas</s> and householders, pressing out their very skin, flesh, and blood, give gifts and make merit, still the monks should use [these] with moderation and mindful consideration.' Having understood this, he went through <s>Vaiśālī</s> for alms. Having finished his meal and returned from his alms-round, he put away his bowl and robe, washed his feet, and entered the monastery for seclusion. Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, emerging from seclusion in the evening, sat on the seat prepared before the community of monks.

children.text: ) niṣadya bhagavān bhikṣūn āmantrayate sma / ihāhaṃ bhikṣavaḥ pūrvāhṇe nivāsya pātracīvaram ādāya vaiśālīṃ piṇḍāya prāvikṣam* / adrākṣam ahaṃ bhikṣavaḥ saṃbahulān bhikṣūn ārāmadvāre aśucimrakṣitāni śayanāsanāni śocayata ātapayataḥ praviṣajataḥ / dṛṣṭvā ca punar me etad abhavat* / yad api śrāddhā brāhmaṇagṛhapatayaḥ prapīḍya prapīḍya tvaṅmāṃsaśoṇitaṃ dānāni dadati puṇyāni kurvanti tad api bhikṣavo mātrayā pratisaṃkhyāya paribhuṃjante / sādhu bhikṣavaḥ śraddhādeyasya mātrāparibhojitāyāḥ kāla
children.translated_text: Having sat down, the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the monks: 'Here, monks, in the forenoon, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered <s>Vaiśālī</s> for alms. I saw many monks at the monastery gate cleaning, airing, and drying bedding and seating soiled with impurities. Having seen this, I reflected: "Although faithful <s>brāhmaṇas</s> and householders, pressing out their very skin, flesh, and blood, give gifts and make merit, still the monks should use [these] with moderation and mindful consideration." It is good, monks, that what is given in faith be used with moderation, with timeliness,
with
appropriate frequency, with reckoning, and with measure.'
[MSV II 89]

children.text: ) atha bhagavāñ chraddhādeyasya mātrādiparibhojitānāṃ varṇaṃ bhāṣitvā bhikṣūn amantrayate sma / tasmāt tarhi bhikṣavo na vinā pratyāstaraṇena sāṃghikaṃ śayanāsanaṃ paribhoktavyam aśucimrakṣitaṃ śayanāsanaṃ ca / tatkṣaṇād eva śocayitavyam anyathā sātisāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having praised the use with moderation and so forth of what is given in faith, addressed the monks: 'Therefore, monks, communal bedding and seating should not be used without a bed-spread. And bedding and seating soiled with impurities should be cleaned immediately. Otherwise, there is an offense.'

body.translated_text: Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, after dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s> as long as he pleased, set out on a journey toward <s>Vaiśālī</s>. Traveling by stages, he arrived at <s>Vaiśālī</s>. In <s>Vaiśālī</s> he was dwelling on the bank of the Monkey Pond in the Pinnacled Hall. Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered <s>Vaiśālī</s> for alms.

body.text: atha bhagavān pūrvāhṇe nivāsya pātracīvaram ādāya vaiśālīṃ piṇḍāya prāvikṣad āyuṣmatānandena paścācchramaṇena / adrākṣīd bhagavān anyataraṃ puruṣaṃ kālakapṛṣṭham* / dūrād eva dṛṣṭvā ca punar āyuṣmantam ānandam āmantrayate / paśyasi tvam ānanda etaṃ puruṣaṃ kālakapṛṣṭham* / evaṃ bhadanta / eṣa ānanda puruṣaḥ kāśyapasya samyaksaṃbuddhasya pravacane pravrajita āsīt* / tatrānena sāṃghikaṃ śayanāsanaṃ kalpapratyāstaraṇena malapratyāstaraṇena paṭṭikāṃ surucikāṃ loḍhakaṃ kṛtvā paribhuktam* / tasya karmaṇo vipākena paṃca janmaśatāni kālakaprṣṭho jātaḥ / yāvad etarhy api kālakapṛṣṭho jāta iti / viditvā vaiśālīṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pūrvavad yāvat pratisaṃlayanād vyūtthāya purastād bhikṣusaṃghasya prajñapta evāsane niṣaṇṇaḥ / niṣadya bhagavān bhikṣūn āmantrayate sma / adyāhaṃ bhikṣavaḥ pūrvāhṇe nivāsya pātracīvaram ādāya vaiśālīṃ piṇḍāya (

children.translated_text: [MSV II 90]

children.text: ) praviṣṭaḥ / tatrāham adrākṣaṃ puruṣaṃ kālakapṛṣṭham* / sa kāśyapasya samyaksaṃbuddhasya pravacane bhikṣur āsīt* / tatrānena sāṃghikaṃ śayanāsanaṃ kalpapratyāstaraṇena pūrvavad yāvat paṃca janmaśatāni kālakapṛṣṭho jātaḥ / tasmāt tarhi bhikṣavo 'dyāgreṇa na bhikṣuṇā kalpapratyāstaraṇena sāṃghikaṃ śayanāsanaṃ paribhoktavyam* / paribhuṃkte / sātisāraḥ / api tu dvābhyāṃ pratyāstaraṇābhyāṃ paribhoktavyaṃ ghanena vā ekapuṭena / pailottikena vā dvipuṭena /
children.translated_text: There I saw a man with a dark-spotted back. He was a monk in the dispensation of <s>Kāśyapa</s>, the Perfectly Enlightened One. There, he used communal bedding and seating with a soiled cover-spread, as before, for five hundred births he was born with a dark-spotted back. Therefore, monks, from this day forward, a monk should not use communal bedding and seating with a soiled cover-spread. If he does, there is an offense. Rather, one should use it with two cover-spreads: either a thick single-layered one, or a patchwork double-layered one.'

body.translated_text: Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe and entered <s>Vaiśālī</s> for alms, with the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> following behind as attendant. The <s>Bhagavān</s> saw a certain man with a dark-spotted back. Having seen him from afar, he addressed the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>: 'Do you see, <s>Ānanda</s>, this man with a dark-spotted back?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir.' 'This man, <s>Ānanda</s>, was a renunciant in the dispensation of <s>Kāśyapa</s>, the Perfectly Enlightened One. There, he used communal bedding and seating with a soiled cover-spread, making [it into] a strip-cover, a fine spread, and a rug. As the ripening of that deed, for five hundred births he has been born with a dark-spotted back. Even now he is born with a dark-spotted back.' Having understood this, he went through <s>Vaiśālī</s> for alms, as before, up to the point where, emerging from seclusion, he sat on the seat prepared before the community of monks. Having sat down, the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the monks: 'Today, monks, in the forenoon, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered <s>Vaiśālī</s> for alms.

body.text: bhikṣavaś citropacitrāṇi pratyāstaraṇāni dhārayanti dīrghadaśāni / brāhmaṇagṛhapatayo 'vadhyāyanti kṣipanti vivācayanti / bhagavān āha / nīlaṃ kardamaṃ kaṣāyaṃ vā pratyāstaraṇaṃ śastralūnaṃ kṛtvā dhārayitavyam* / anyathā sātisāraḥ /
body.translated_text: Monks were keeping colorful and multi-colored cover-spreads with long fringes. <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> and householders disparaged, criticized, and censured them. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'A cover-spread should be dyed blue, mud-colored, or brown, cut with a blade, and then kept. Otherwise, there is an offense.'

children.translated_text: Monks were afflicted with a skin disease

children.text: ) bādhyante / tasya cīvarakāṇi pūyaśoṇitopaliptāni durgandhitāni makṣikākīrṇāni / sa piṇḍapātaṃ praviṣṭaḥ / taṃ dṛṣṭvā brāhmaṇagṛhapatayo 'vadhyāyanti kṣipanti vivācayanti / etat prakaraṇaṃ bhikṣavo bhagavata ārocayanti / bhagavān āha / tasmād anujānāmi kaṇḍūpracchādanaṃ dhārayitavyam* / paṃcabhiḥ ṣaḍbhir vā divasaiḥ śocayitavyam* / anyathā sātisāraḥ /
children.translated_text: (<s>kuṇḍūroga</s>). Their robes were smeared with pus and blood, foul-smelling, and covered with flies. One [such monk] went out for alms. Seeing him, <s>brāhmaṇas</s> and householders disparaged, criticized, and censured him. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore I permit: an itch-covering cloth should be worn. It should be washed every five or six days. Otherwise, there is an offense.'

children.translated_text: [MSV II 91]

children.text: ) tān dṛṣṭvā brāhmaṇagṛhapatayo 'vadhyāyanti kṣipanti vivācayanti / etat prakaraṇaṃ bhikṣavo bhagavata ārocayanti / bhagavān āha / kuṣṭharogābhibhūtasyāhaṃ bhikṣavo bhikṣor āsamudācārikān dharmān prajñāpayiṣyāmi / kuṣṭharogābhibhūtena bhikṣuṇā sāṃghikam śayanāsanaṃ layanaṃ ca na paribhoktavyam* / prāsādādiṣu yathāparikīrtiteṣu sthāneṣu sthātavyam* / sāmghikī prasrāvakuṭī varcaḥkuṭī ca na praveṣṭavyā / pratigupte sthāne saṃghena tasya vāso deyaḥ / upasthānaṃ ca kartavyam* / kuṣṭharogābhibhūto bhikṣur yathāprajñaptān āsamudācārikān dharmān na samādāya vartate saṃgho vā sātisāro bhavati /
children.translated_text: Seeing them, <s>brāhmaṇas</s> and householders disparaged, criticized, and censured them. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'I shall prescribe rules of proper conduct for a monk afflicted with leprosy. A monk afflicted with leprosy should not use communal bedding, seating, or lodging. He should not stand in the aforementioned places such as upper stories and so forth. He should not use the communal toilet or outhouse. The <s>Saṅgha</s> should provide him with a dwelling in a secluded place. And attendance should be provided for him. If a monk afflicted with leprosy does not observe the prescribed rules of proper conduct, or the <s>Saṅgha</s> [fails to provide], there is an offense.'

body.translated_text: Monks were afflicted with leprosy (<s>kuṣṭharoga</s>). They used communal bedding and seating. They remained in the upper stories, at the pool, in the gate-chamber, in the surrounding area, on the walking paths, and at the assembly trees—foul-smelling, covered with flies.

body.text: āyuṣmān upālī buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ pṛcchati / labhyaṃ bhadanta sugatacīvaram atirekacīvarakalpena dhārayitum* / na labhyam upālin* / labhyaṃ bhadanta kauśeyaṃ cīvaraṃ tricīvarādhiṣṭhānena atirekacīvarādhiṣṭhānena dhārayitum* / labhyam upālin yatheṣṭhataḥ / evaṃ pūrṇakaṃ śāṇakaṃ labhyam /
body.translated_text: The Venerable <s>Upāli</s> asked the Buddha, the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'Is it permissible, Venerable Sir, to keep a <s>Sugata</s>-robe under the designation of an extra robe?' 'It is not permissible, <s>Upāli</s>.' 'Is it permissible, Venerable Sir, to keep a silk robe under the designation of the triple-robe set or under the designation of an extra robe?' 'It is permissible, <s>Upāli</s>, as one wishes.' Likewise for hemp-cloth and bark-cloth—it is permissible.

body.text: uddānam* /
body.translated_text: Summary verse:

body.text:
bhāṅgeyaṃ keśacīvaraṃ nāgnyaṃ keśalucanaṃ parṇaśāṭīm* /
ajinaṃ sāntarottaraṃ tirīṭim aṅganīlakam* /
body.translated_text: 'A hemp [robe], a hair-robe, nudity, hair-plucking, a leaf-garment, an antelope-skin with upper and inner garment, bark-cloth, and body-painting with blue.'

children.translated_text: Standing to one side, that monk said to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'I wish, Venerable Sir, to wear a hemp robe.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'That is a mark of heretics, foolish man—namely, a hemp robe. Therefore, a monk should not wear a hemp robe. If he does, there is an offense.'

body.translated_text: The setting is <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Then a certain monk approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, he saluted the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s feet with his head and stood to one side.

body.translated_text: Another monk went and said to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'I wish, Venerable Sir, to wear a hair-robe.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'That is a mark of heretics, foolish man.' As before, up to: there is an offense.

The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Monks, it is not only now; in the past too, through the fault of shamelessness, he failed to obtain the maiden. Listen to this!

body.translated_text: Another monk said to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'I wish, Venerable Sir, to adopt nudity.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'That is a mark of heretics, foolish man—namely, nudity. He began to dance, spreading his tail-fan. <s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s> saw him. He said: 'Why does he dance?' Others informed him: 'Your daughter has chosen him.' He said: 'This one is devoid of shame and modesty. I shall not give my daughter to him.' When the peacock heard this, he went before <s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s> and spoke this verse:

body.translated_text: In the past, monks, there was a swan-king named <s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s>. His daughter descended for a self-choice ceremony (<s>svayaṃvara</s>). Having heard, birds from various regions and directions gathered. Each one thought: 'She will choose me.' The

body.text: kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ / yo 'sau mayūraḥ eṣa evāsau bhikṣus tena kālena tena samayena / tadāpy eṣa ahrīkyadoṣād dārikām alabhamāno duḥkhī durmanā pakṣiṇamadhyād avakrāntaḥ / etarhy apy asau nāgnyam albhamāno duḥkhī durmanā bhikṣusaṃghamadhyāt prakrāntaḥ /
body.translated_text: What do you think, <s>bhikṣus</s>? That peacock was none other than this very <s>bhikṣu</s> at that time and on that occasion. Then too, because of the fault of shamelessness, unable to obtain the girl, he departed from the midst of the birds, miserable and dejected. Now too, unable to obtain a wife, he has departed from the midst of the <s>bhikṣu-saṃgha</s>, miserable and dejected.

If he does, he commits a transgression (<s>sātisāra</s>).' (

body.text: āyuṣmān plīhakānandaḥ anyatamasminn abhikṣuke āvāse akavāṭake varṣā upagataḥ / tasya bahir nigatasya saṃghāṭy upahṛtā / etad yāvad bhagavān āha / na bhikṣuṇā abhikṣuke āvāse akavāṭake varṣā upagantavyam* / na ca vinā saṃghāṭyā kvacid gantavyam* / gacchati / sātisāro bhavati /
body.translated_text: The Venerable <s>Plīhakānanda</s> spent the rainy season in a certain monastery without monks and without doors. While he was away, his <s>saṃghāṭī</s> (outer robe) was stolen. This matter was reported to the <s>Bhagavān</s>, who said: 'A <s>bhikṣu</s> should not spend the rainy season in a monastery without monks and without doors. Nor should one go anywhere without the <s>saṃghāṭī</s>. If one does, he commits a transgression.'

body.text: āyuṣmān plīhakānando glānaḥ / tasyāyuṣmān ānando glānopasthāyakaḥ / devaś ca varṣitum ārabdhaḥ / sa notsahate saṃghāṭīṃ prāvṛtya gantum* / (

Others departed without being designated. No one accepts for them. Monks do not accept due to scruples. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'It should be accepted. No scruples need be entertained here.' Another case: the share is too small to divide. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Having combined it with other goods, the monastery residents should divide it. No scruples need be entertained here.' One who has been designated for a family donation does not accept it. He should be made to pay a fine of five <s>paṇas</s> (coins).

body.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> had said that the robe-distribution should be given to the monks. Monks depart on a journey through the countryside after the <s>saṃgha</s>'s invitation ceremony. No one takes their share. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'One should look for a monk who will accept his share, and then go.' Other monks also accept without being designated. Mutual conflict arose among the monks. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'A <s>bhikṣu</s> should not accept a share without being designated. If he does, he commits a transgression.' Yet other monks, though designated, accept and then do not take [their share]. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'They should be made to pay the full amount.' When novices depart, no one accepts their share. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Their teachers and preceptors should accept it.' Monks distribute the family donations (

children.translated_text: ) It was the practice of the Group of Six. The gate of <s>Jetavana</s> was never empty — one or another of the Group of Six was always there. <s>Upananda</s> was standing at the gate of <s>Jetavana</s>. He saw the monk from a distance — crane-like head, drooping eyebrows. He reflected: 'Some elder monk is coming. I shall go to meet him.' He went out to meet him. 'Welcome, welcome, elder!' 'I bow to you, teacher.' He reflected: 'This one knows neither teacher nor preceptor. He is simply old.' Knowing this, he said: 'Kinsman, where do you come from?' 'From such-and-such a town.' 'Is there a monastery there?' 'There is.' 'Is it a monastery or a ruin?' The monk told him everything in detail. 'Why have you come?' 'I am bringing monks to share a meal.' 'If so, I myself shall come out of compassion for you.' 'Teacher, excellent.' <s>Upananda</s> reflected: 'If this one goes elsewhere from me, he will spread the word widely. He must be kept under close watch.' He entertained the monk, gave him an after-hours drink, and engaged him in conversation until it was past the proper time. A comfortable bed was prepared. Foot-washing and foot-ointment were provided. He stayed with him until sleep overcame the old monk. children.translated_text: ) He asked the second one and said: 'Kinsman, what have you done here?' 'Elder, I have given regular <s>Dharma</s> teachings here at the proper times.' 'Kinsman, if gains could be obtained by <s>Dharma</s> teaching, <s>Upananda</s> would teach the <s>Dharma</s> at all times—standing, walking, sitting. Whatever gain has accrued here, all of it is due to the influence of that other kinsman. For by him this monastery is constantly sprinkled and swept. And a delicate young woman has been provided to spread cow-dung. The Blessed One has declared five benefits of sweeping. Which five? One's own mind is purified. Others' minds are purified. The deities are delighted. One accumulates a root of merit conducive to a pleasing [rebirth]. At the breaking up of the body, one is reborn among the gods in the heavenly world. Thus, by the sweeping of this monastery, the donors have been inspired with faith. And the deities have become delighted. Therefore, gains have accrued here through his influence. Whatever he gives should be accepted, not questioned.' He too, rebuked and shamed, stood silent. Having silenced both of them, he said: 'Kinsmen, is there another method? Let us make a formal motion and divide.' 'The Blessed One has said that a formal motion is irrevocable.' Those two, already rebuked, said: 'Elder, do as you wish.' Then <s>Upananda</s> made three portions. He sat himself between two portions. Having placed one portion between the two of them, he began to make a formal motion: 'Listen, you two kinsmen: two. body.translated_text: In a certain small town, there was a householder. He had built a monastery. If a hundred monks resided there, he would give a hundred cloth-pieces. Likewise, even if only one monk resided there, he would give a hundred cloth-pieces all the same. At another time, two elderly monks spent the rainy season in that very monastery. The householder sent a hundred cloth-pieces. Having received them, the two deliberated with each other. One said: 'This is the property of the <s>saṃgha</s> (community); it should be surrendered.' The other said: 'It belongs to us alone.' 'If so, take it.' He said: 'Let there be no mutual conflict.' Neither one took it. They deliberated again: 'How should we proceed here?' One said: 'Let monks be summoned. We shall divide it with them.' The other said: 'So be it. Who shall go?' 'The junior one.' 'Who shall guard the cloth?' 'The junior one.' 'That won't work. (

Then they made an agreement: "Let one of us go by the water and the other by the bank. Whatever is obtained, let it be our common [property]." Thereupon one set out by the water and the other by the bank. The fish frightened by the one in the water climbed onto the bank—the one on the bank killed them. The one in the water killed those in the water. A great heap of fish accumulated. One said: "You divide." The other said: "I will not divide." "Why not?" "Lest there be a fault on my part." He said: "Nephews, why do you stand so worried?" "Uncle, we have obtained fish. Why don't you divide them?" "Uncle, for fear of fault." "You two are afraid of fault—what do you want?" "<s>Pūrṇamukha</s>, whoever cheats will fall headlong into hell." <s>Pūrṇamukha</s> reflected: "These two united must be separated." Then, having observed their regular habits and established work, he approached one of them and asked: "Nephew, what have you done here?" "Uncle, I went by the water. The fish frightened by my going through the water climbed onto the bank—he killed those." children.translated_text: He said: 'Even if a monk has entered the rainy-season retreat relying upon a cowshed, if <s>brāhmaṇas</s> and householders there, with the <s>Saṅgha</s> in mind, give offerings, whether small or great, to whoever dwells there—whether one, two, or many—those [offerings] belong to them alone. There should be no remorse in this matter.'

body.translated_text: The setting is <s>Śrāvastī</s>. In a certain small town, a householder [lived]. He had built a monastery. There, one monk had taken up the rains retreat. He was diligent and industrious. By him, that monastery was daily plastered and swept. Moreover, that monastery was established on a beautiful, secluded, and spacious piece of ground, adorned with various trees, resounding with the calls of geese, herons, peacocks, parrots, mynahs, and cuckoos, beautified with various flowers and fruits. A wealthy caravan-leader, on his travels, spent a night in that monastery. Having seen the beauty of the monastery and the beauty of the garden, filled with faith, without even seeing [the monks], he sent abundant gifts addressed to the <s>Saṅgha</s> of monks. He departed that very night. That monk, being scrupulous, [thought:] 'This gain belongs to the <s>Saṅgha</s>.' Out of scrupulousness, he would not accept it. He began searching for monks to divide it among. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One (

The monks said to them: 'Venerable ones, your teacher obtained five hundred pieces of cloth from that householder. Those were distributed among us alone. Now too, this offering should come to us alone.' They replied: 'Our teacher is known to be of great merit. Perhaps at some time he would have agreed to share with you.' [The monks] began to argue. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Monks, there are eight [types of] gains. What eight? A gain brought by the boundary (<s>sīmā</s>); a gain brought by arrangement; a gain brought by dependence; a gain designated by the <s>Saṅgha</s>; a gain designated by a monk; a rainy-season gain; a face-to-face gain; and a redirected gain.'

body.translated_text: In a certain market-town there was a householder. He had a monastery built, fully furnished with all requisites. He left those five hundred pieces of cloth at that very monastery and departed. body.translated_text: 'What is a gain brought by the boundary? As in the case where there is one communal dwelling and one <s>poṣadha</s> (observance ceremony). Whatever gain comes to be given at that very monastery is to be used by the monks residing there alone, because of the single <s>poṣadha</s>. This is called a gain brought by the boundary.'

body.translated_text: 'What is a gain designated by the <s>Saṅgha</s>? A gain that is fixed and undisputed. This is called a gain designated by the <s>Saṅgha</s>.'

body.translated_text: 'What is a gain designated by a monk? A gain that is fixed and undisputed, designated for a lodging, a cell, or an upper chamber. Whichever monk resides there, it belongs to him alone. This is called a gain designated by a monk.'

body.text: vārṣiko lābhaḥ katamaḥ / yo lābho varṣoṣitasya bhikṣusaṃghasya dāyikaiḥ prajñaptaḥ / ayam ucyate vārṣiko lābhaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'What is a rainy-season gain? A gain designated by donors for the community of monks that has completed the rainy-season retreat. This is called a rainy-season gain.'

body.text: saṃmukhalābhaḥ katamaḥ / yo lābho 'niyato 'vipaṃcitaḥ / ayam ucyate saṃmukhalābhaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'What is a face-to-face gain? A gain that is unfixed and undisputed. This is called a face-to-face gain.'

body.text: pratyādeśalābhaḥ katamaḥ / yo lābho jātau bodhau dharmacakre parinirvāṇe niryātitaḥ / sacen na śakyate caturmahācaityeṣu ekasminn eva mahācaitye deyo nānayatra / ayam ucyate pratyādeśalābhaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'What is a redirected gain? A gain that is dedicated at the [occasion of the Buddha's] birth, enlightenment, turning of the Dharma-wheel, or <s>parinirvāṇa</s>. If it cannot be given at all four great <s>caityas</s> (shrines), it should be given at a single great <s>caitya</s> and not elsewhere. This is called a redirected gain.'

children.translated_text: 'You death-stick wielder, what kind of man are you? I shall place my foot on your throat and drink the ghee, and I shall live!' The physician, saying 'Hmph!' departed angrily. Then <s>Upananda</s>, having filled a bowl with ghee, drank it. He died of dysentery. He had accumulated much gold—three hundred thousand gold pieces. The first [hundred thousand] from [trading] bowls and robes. The second from medicines for the sick. The third from various transactions. The ministers heard and reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, the Venerable <s>Upananda</s> has died. He has much gold—three hundred thousand gold pieces. May Your Majesty give orders regarding it.' The king said: 'If so, go and seal his dwelling.' The monks took him [the body] to the cremation ground. Having come, they [the ministers] sealed the dwelling. The monks, having cremated him at the burning ground, returned to the monastery. They saw the dwelling sealed with the royal seal. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. Or at the time of your wedding celebrations, do you at that time look to <s>Upananda</s>? Has <s>Upananda</s> ever been invited by you for life with robe, almsfood, bedding, and medicine for the sick? Or has attendance upon the sick <s>Upananda</s> been rendered [by you]?" 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> assented to the Blessed One and went to King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s>. Having approached, he conveyed the message as instructed. The king said: 'Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>, let it be as the Blessed One commands. I withdraw my involvement.' Then the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> conveyed the king's reply to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Distribute, monks, the deceased property of the monk <s>Upananda</s>.' The monks brought it into the assembly, sold it, and distributed [the proceeds]. body.translated_text: The setting is <s>Śrāvastī</s>. A boil appeared on <s>Upananda</s>'s head. He went to a physician. 'Good sir, prescribe medicine for me.' He said: 'Noble one, drink a draught of ghee. You will recover.' <s>Upananda</s> reflected: 'If I drink today, I will recover today itself. Tomorrow, by what pretext shall I collect ghee or cloth? As long as I can collect by a suitable pretext, I shall drink afterwards.' He was a man of great merit among his relatives. He sent his co-residents and pupils in all directions. They collected an abundance of ghee-pots and cloths for wound-bandaging. On the second day, the physician came and asked: 'Noble one, are you well? Have you drunk the ghee?' 'Good sir, I have not drunk it.' 'Noble one, that was not good. Now drink double the amount.' He told his co-residents and pupils: 'Have you heard what the physician said? Teacher, (

body.translated_text: The monks, filled with doubt, asked the <s>Buddha</s>, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubt: 'See, Venerable Sir, the Venerable <s>Upananda</s> was ruined by excessive greed.' The Blessed One said: 'Not only now, monks. In the past too he was ruined by excessive greed. Listen to this.'

body.translated_text: Other monks of great renown and merit died. They had many requisites—both monastic requisites and livelihood requisites. [These] were brought to the senior seat. The Blessed One had said: 'The attendant should take six requisites.' He, picking and choosing, took the finest. The Blessed One said: 'The finest should not be given.' The monks gave the coarsest. The Blessed One said: 'The coarsest should not be given. Rather, the middling should be given.'

body.translated_text: Sick monks died unknowingly on communal bedding. The Blessed One said: 'The attendant of the sick should be skilled in observing the condition of the sick one. He should be checked frequently. He should not be negligent in his duties. Having assessed the physical condition, the sick monk should be moved by some pretext to personal bedding and laid down [there].'

body.translated_text: At that time, a certain monk was ailing, suffering, severely ill. He was of little renown. He had no medicine. Having assessed his physical condition, he said to his attendant: 'I have nothing. Make offerings on my behalf.' He agreed. The monk died. He was reborn in the lower realms. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'That monk who died, monks—what did he say to his attendant?' They reported the events as they had occurred. 'That monk has fallen into the lower realms, monks. If his fellow practitioners had made an offering to the Three Jewels on his behalf, his mind would have been filled with faith. Therefore a monk should not neglect a sick fellow practitioner. An attendant for the sick should be provided. If there is no medicine for him, having asked him, (

children.translated_text: ) a dense forest. Burning with the fire of anger, it set that dense forest ablaze. Burned right there, having harbored ill will toward the monks, it was reborn in the hells. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Be disgusted, monks, with all forms of existence! Be disgusted with all causes of rebirth in any form of existence! For here, the body of a single being was burned in three places: in the dense forest by the fire of anger; in hell by the hellish fire; and in the cremation ground by ordinary fire. Therefore monks should not develop excessive attachment to their requisites. In whomever it arises, that should be abandoned. If he does not abandon it, he commits an offense. Moreover, if a sick monk asks for his own requisite, the attendant should give it promptly. If he does not give it, he commits an offense.'

body.translated_text: The setting is <s>Śrāvastī</s>. At that time, a certain sick monk died in his cell. That monk was taken to the burning ground, the funeral rites were performed, and he was cremated. Then [the monks] returned to the monastery. The robe-distributor entered his cell. He, having picked up a club, stood up: 'First give a <s>Dharma</s> teaching dedicated to me, then distribute the robes.' The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: 'Having given a <s>Dharma</s> teaching dedicated to him and having dedicated the merit, afterward the robes should be distributed.'

The Blessed One remained outside, having had the alms-food brought out. For five reasons do <s>Buddhas</s>, Blessed Ones, remain outside with the alms-food brought out. Which five? They wish to be in solitary meditation. They wish to teach the <s>Dharma</s> to the deities. They wish to inspect the sleeping quarters. They wish to look in on the sick. They wish to establish a training rule of the <s>Vinaya</s> for the disciples. The Blessed One generated a worldly thought: 'Oh, if only <s>Śakra</s>, lord of the gods, would bring water from Lake <s>Anavatapta</s> and earth from Mount <s>Gandhamādana</s>!' Now it is a law of nature that when the Blessed One generates a worldly thought, at that very moment <s>Śakra</s>, <s>Brahmā</s>, and the other gods know the Blessed One's thought. Then <s>Śakra</s>, lord of the gods, taking a golden pitcher of water endowed with eight qualities from Lake <s>Anavatapta</s> and earth from Mount <s>Gandhamādana</s>, quickly appeared before the Blessed One. He said: 'Let the Blessed One wait—I shall attend to him.' The Blessed One said: 'He did not go forth for <s>Kauśika</s>'s sake, but for mine. Moreover, have you not seen him before? Stand aside—gods are fastidious. I myself shall attend to him.' Then the Blessed One, having tied up his robe, with the hand born of innumerable hundreds of merits, marked with the <s>cakra</s>, <s>svastika</s>, and <s>nandyāvarta</s>, the hand that gives reassurance to the frightened—grasped that monk, lifted him out of urine and excrement, and placed him to one side. He scraped him clean with a bamboo splint, rubbed him with white clay, and bathed him. Then
he was settled.

body.translated_text: Then the Blessed One, knowing that the <s>Saṅgha</s> of monks had recently departed, taking the key, went walking about from monastery to monastery, from dwelling to dwelling, from chamber to chamber, from walkway to walkway, inspecting [everything]. He came upon a certain old dwelling. There, a severely ill monk, of little renown, lay submerged in his own urine and excrement. Seeing the Blessed One, he cried out: 'I am without a protector, Blessed One! I am without a protector, <s>Sugata</s>!' The Blessed One said: 'Why do you, a monk who went forth under me, the protector of the three worlds, cry out thus: "I am without a protector, Blessed One! I am without a protector, <s>Sugata</s>!"?' body.translated_text: Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, these sick monks have no mother, no father, no other relative—none other than you, their fellow practitioners. Therefore, fellow practitioners should attend to one another. body.translated_text: 'Once upon a time, monks, in a certain hermitage abounding in flowers, fruits, and water, adorned with various trees, there dwelt a seer possessed of the five superknowledges. He attended to his disciple. The disciple recovered. Then by him the five superknowledges were realized. What do you think, monks? That seer at that time and on that occasion was none other than I. That disciple of the seer is this very monk. Then too I attended to him; now too I have attended to him.'

It was the practice of that king: a bell was always hung at the gate, announcing petitioners. Whenever a petitioner stood at the gate, the bell would ring. Then that bell, announcing the arrival of the <s>Pratyekabuddha</s>, began to ring. The prince said: 'Mother, father, a petitioner has come. Let it be investigated what he requests.' They said: 'Son, over twelve years we have collected the ingredients and prepared this ghee. Drink it first; afterward we shall admit the petitioner and inquire what he requests.' But he, filled with curiosity and eager for an auspicious beginning, about to drink the ghee, his body struck at a vital point by the distress of the petitioner's vessel of hope — this arrangement did not please him. He said: 'Mother, father, I shall not partake until the petitioner enters.' The king gave the order to the door-keeper: 'Admit the petitioner.' He was admitted. The prince saw him — pleasing in body and pleasing in mind, having entered with a calm deportment. He said: 'What does the noble one need?' The other told him everything in detail. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: '<s>Bhikṣus</s>, in earlier births, <s>karmas</s> were performed by them, accumulated, gathered in their requisites, ripened in their conditions, standing ready like a flood, inevitably coming to fruition. <s>Bhikṣus</s>, <s>karmas</s> performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element. Rather, <s>karmas</s> performed ripen in the elements of the body itself — in the <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), <s>dhātus</s> (elements), and <s>āyatanas</s> (sense-bases) — whether wholesome or unwholesome.

body.translated_text: The setting is <s>Śrāvastī</s>. At that time in <s>Śrāvastī</s>, there was a householder named <s>Śreṣṭhin</s> — wealthy, of great riches, of great possessions, with vast and extensive property, rivaling the wealth of <s>Vaiśravaṇa</s>, competing with the riches of <s>Vaiśravaṇa</s>. He had brought a wife from a family equal to his own. Being childless and desiring a son, he prayed to <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Varuṇa</s>, <s>Kubera</s>, <s>Śakra</s>, <s>Brahmā</s>, and other special deities — namely, garden deities, forest deities, crossroad deities, intersection deities, deities receiving offerings, innate deities, co-religious deities, and ever-present deities. There is indeed this popular saying: that through prayer, sons and daughters are born. But this is not so. If it were, each person would have a thousand sons, as does a <s>Cakravartin</s> king. Rather, it is from the conjunction of three conditions that sons and daughters are born. Which three? The mother and father are passionate; they have come together; and the mother is healthy and in her fertile period; and a <s>gandharva</s> (being seeking rebirth) has appeared. From the conjunction of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born. When even through propitiating deities neither son nor daughter [came], then, having rejected all deities, he became devoted to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. He approached a certain <s>bhikṣu</s>. As for jewels—excluding pearls, from gems and lapis lazuli down to those that turn to the right—two shares should be made: one for the Dharma, and the second for the <s>Saṅgha</s>. That which belongs to the Dharma should be used for copying the Buddha's word, or for furnishing a lion-throne. That which belongs to the <s>Saṅgha</s> should be distributed among the monks. As for books—books containing the Buddha's word should not be divided but should be deposited in the storage chest of the <s>Saṅgha</s> of the four directions. Books of non-Buddhist treatises should be sold by the monks and the proceeds distributed. Documents of obligation that can be quickly settled—at the time of property division, these should be distributed among the monks. Those that cannot be [settled] should be deposited in the storage chest of the <s>Saṅgha</s> of the four directions. Gold, silver, and other wrought and unwrought [valuables]—three shares should be made: one for the Buddha, the second for the Dharma, and the third for the <s>Saṅgha</s>. That which belongs to the Buddha should be used for repairs and maintenance of the fragrance-chamber and the <s>stūpas</s> for hair and nail relics. He was invited for another morning meal by another. And another. Another said: 'The Venerable one must eat at my place.' And another. Another said: 'The Venerable one must drink the afternoon beverage at my place.' And another. And others said likewise. Out of consideration for them, he took a little from each for the morning meal.
